\chapter{Very Good, Very Bad}
\label{ch:te-very-good-very-bad}
\hlchaptermodality{76}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that something is very good, bad, easy or difficult in Telugu, and make an adjective the whole comment.}

Complete TE-C76-difficult and demonstrate the chapter promise.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[cālā manci]{\te{చాలా} \te{మంచి} (cālā manci) — very good}

\label{lesson:TE-C76-very}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{saṁvatsaraṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{చాలా} \te{మంచి}}
\textbf{\te{చాలా} \te{మంచి}} (\emph{cālā manci}) — \textquotedblleft{}very good\textquotedblright{}. The new word in it is \textbf{\te{చాలా}}, \textquotedblleft{}very, a lot\textquotedblright{}.

Until now every adjective you had was flat: \te{పెద్ద} was big and there was no bigger. \te{చాలా} is the dial.

It stands in front of what it strengthens: \textbf{\te{చాలా} \te{పెద్ద}} \textquotedblleft{}very big\textquotedblright{}, \textbf{\te{చాలా} \te{కొత్త}} \textquotedblleft{}very new\textquotedblright{}. It also works on its own for \textquotedblleft{}a lot\textquotedblright{}, where \te{కొంచెం} was \textquotedblleft{}a little\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A degree, on any adjective you have.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{cālā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{cālā}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} put \emph{cālā} in front of \emph{manci}, then in front of \emph{pedda}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{lēdā}, then \emph{madhyāhnam}, then say \emph{cālā manci}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{చాలా} \te{మంచి} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}very good\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ceḍḍa]{\te{చెడ్డ} (ceḍḍa) — bad}

\label{lesson:TE-C76-bad}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{cālā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{చెడ్డ}}
\textbf{\te{చెడ్డ}} (\emph{ceḍḍa}) — \textquotedblleft{}bad\textquotedblright{}.

\te{మంచి}, \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{}, has stood without an opposite ever since the adjectives chapter. \te{చెడ్డ} is the opposite.

It sits in front of its noun and does not change, exactly as \te{మంచి} does. Do not reach for \te{చేదు} from the last chapter: that is \emph{bitter}, a taste, and it does not judge anything.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Both ends of the judgement: \te{మంచి} and \te{చెడ్డ}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ceḍḍa}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ceḍḍa}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{manci}, then \emph{ceḍḍa}, then \emph{cālā ceḍḍa}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{enduku}, then \emph{śubhōdayam}, then say \emph{ceḍḍa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{చెడ్డ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}bad\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mancidi]{\te{మంచిది} (mancidi) — it is a good one}

\label{lesson:TE-C76-itisgood}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ceḍḍa} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{మంచిది}}
\textbf{\te{మంచిది}} (\emph{mancidi}) — \textquotedblleft{}it is a good one\textquotedblright{}.

You could already say \textbf{\te{మంచి} \te{పుస్తకం}}, \textquotedblleft{}a good book\textquotedblright{}. You could not yet say that the book \emph{is} good, because a Telugu adjective cannot end a sentence by itself.

Add \textbf{-\te{ది}} and it becomes a thing: \te{మంచి} + \te{ది} = \textquotedblleft{}a good one\textquotedblright{}. \textbf{\te{పుస్తకం} \te{మంచిది}} — \textquotedblleft{}the book is a good one\textquotedblright{}, which is how Telugu says \textquotedblleft{}the book is good\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: -\te{ది} turns a describing word into a naming word}]
Telugu will not let a bare adjective be the predicate. \textbf{-\te{ది}} makes it one — a pronoun-like ending meaning \textquotedblleft{}the one that is\textquotedblright{}. \te{మంచిది} \textquotedblleft{}a good one\textquotedblright{}, \te{చెడ్డది} \textquotedblleft{}a bad one\textquotedblright{}, \te{కొత్తది} \textquotedblleft{}a new one\textquotedblright{}. For a person the ending is \textbf{-\te{వాడు}} or \textbf{-\te{ఆమె}} instead. Learn -\te{ది} now and every adjective you already have can finish a sentence.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
An adjective that can be the whole comment.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mancidi}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mancidi}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{manci pustakaṁ}, then \emph{pustakaṁ mancidi}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{endukaṇṭē}, then \emph{rāyu}, then say \emph{mancidi}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{మంచిది} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}it is a good one\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sulabhaṁ]{\te{సులభం} (sulabhaṁ) — easy}

\label{lesson:TE-C76-easy}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{mancidi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{సులభం}}
\textbf{\te{సులభం}} (\emph{sulabhaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}easy\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \textbf{\te{సు}-} (\textquotedblleft{}well\textquotedblright{}) plus \textbf{\te{లభ}} (\textquotedblleft{}got\textquotedblright{}): what is easily got. The same \te{సు}- is the \te{శు}- of \te{శుభోదయం}, softened.

\textbf{\te{తెలుగు} \te{సులభం}} — \textquotedblleft{}Telugu is easy.\textquotedblright{} A \textbf{-\te{ం}} noun like this needs no -\te{ది}; it is already a naming word.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A verdict you can pass on a task.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sulabhaṁ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sulabhaṁ}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{telugu sulabhaṁ}, then add \emph{cālā} in front of \emph{sulabhaṁ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ivāḷa}, then \emph{tīsukō}, then say \emph{sulabhaṁ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{సులభం} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}easy\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kaṣṭaṁ]{\te{కష్టం} (kaṣṭaṁ) — difficult; trouble}

\label{lesson:TE-C76-difficult}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{sulabhaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{కష్టం}}
\textbf{\te{కష్టం}} (\emph{kaṣṭaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}difficult\textquotedblright{}, and also \textquotedblleft{}trouble, hardship\textquotedblright{}.

The pair to \te{సులభం}, and a Sanskrit tatsama shared right across India.

It carries more weight than English \textquotedblleft{}difficult\textquotedblright{}: \textbf{\te{కష్టం}} said alone about someone's situation means real hardship, not an awkward crossword.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Both ends of a task: \te{సులభం} and \te{కష్టం}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kaṣṭaṁ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kaṣṭaṁ}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{sulabhaṁ}, then \emph{kaṣṭaṁ}, then \emph{cālā kaṣṭaṁ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ninna}, then \emph{kuṭumbaṁ}, then say \emph{kaṣṭaṁ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{కష్టం} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}difficult; trouble\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
